Fix an extension of number fields <MATH_0001> with rings of integers
<MATH_0002> and <MATH_0003>. The injection <MATH_0004> defines a
morphism <MATH_0005>.
As discussed above, the points where <MATH_0006> is unramified in our sense
correspond to the set of points where <MATH_0007> is unramified in the conventional
sense. In the conventional sense, the locus of ramification in
<MATH_0008> can be defined by vanishing set of the
different; this is an ideal in <MATH_0009>. In fact, the different is
nothing but the annihilator of the module
<MATH_0010>. Similarly, the
discriminant is an ideal in <MATH_0011>, namely it is the
norm of the different.
The vanishing set of the discriminant is precisely the set
of points of <MATH_0012> which ramify in <MATH_0013>.
Thus, denoting by <MATH_0014> the complement of the closed subset
defined by the different in <MATH_0015>,
we obtain a morphism <MATH_0016> which is unramified.
Furthermore, this morphism is also flat, as any local homomorphism
of discrete valuation rings is flat, and hence this morphism is
actually <ACCENT_0001>tale. If <MATH_0017> is finite Galois, then denoting by
<MATH_0018> the complement of the closed subset defined by the discriminant in
<MATH_0019>, we see that we get even a
finite <ACCENT_0002>tale morphism <MATH_0020>.
Thus, this is an example of a finite <ACCENT_0003>tale covering.
